v.why: The L2 gradient is alpha*W divided by batch size, so at batches of 4-10 raising alpha imposes a far stronger effective penalty that shrinks weights toward underfitting.
Under standard parameterisation the stable Adam step shrinks with width, so widening at learning rates of 0.077-1 pushes training further into divergence and dead ReLUs.
Strong L2 shrinks every layer, and the shrinkage compounds multiplicatively, so an extra layer under alpha 0.0167-1 collapses activations toward a constant prediction.
Three-layer ReLU nets diverge and lose units at lower learning rates than shallow nets, so increasing the step hurts them more overall.
Wide layers produce larger coordinated output changes per Adam step, so raising the learning rate reaches instability sooner.
Large batches give few updates per epoch, so the step size limits training progress and raising it helps more.
At high learning rates small-batch gradient noise combines with large steps to cause divergence, so a larger batch stabilises training.
When width of 16-40 is the capacity bottleneck, an extra layer supplies missing expressiveness that wide nets do not need.
Nets with widths of 406-1024 have the most excess capacity to overfit small tabular datasets, so added L2 costs them least and may help.
Only in the well-tuned learning-rate band can a deeper net be optimised within 243 epochs; at the extremes depth adds undertraining or divergence.
